samples.L1: Nina rents, and she has saved $92,000: enough for 20% down on a $400,000 home plus closing costs. Last time, her renting twin kept that money in cash, and buying came out ahead in about 3 of every 4 start months since 1991. This time the renting twin invests every dollar she doesn't spend on housing in the whole US stock market, dividends reinvested. We replay the same 307 start months with real US home prices, rents, mortgage rates and stock returns, and every cost of owning. After ten and fifteen years, how often is the buyer still ahead, and what changes if the renter doesn't invest the monthly difference? History, not a forecast: no advice to buy, rent or invest.
samples.L2: "Rent and invest the difference": does it really leave a renter ahead of a homeowner? We take two identical people with the same savings, one who buys a $400,000 home and one who rents and puts the down payment and every month's savings into the whole US stock market, and replay them through 307 real start months since 1991, using real US home prices, rents, mortgage rates and stock returns. The video shows how often the buyer was still ahead after ten and fifteen years, what happens when the renter stops investing the monthly difference, and how the answer moves with the rent you assume. History, not a forecast: no advice to buy, rent or invest.

roles.T: You are an American renter in 2026 with enough saved for a 20% down payment on a home near the national median price. You keep hearing "rent and invest the difference" and wonder whether a renter who invests really ends up ahead of someone who buys.
